newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil town gives new meaning to "party politics".
newsitem.headline: Brazil town gives new meaning to "party politics".

text.p: "Elections," an old man muttered with disdain as a pickup truck, packed with noisy campaign workers and a couple of dancing girls, completed its long, hot journey to the middle of nowhere.

Preparing for Thursday's municipal elections, Brazilian politicians bearing alcohol and music trundled in dusty convoys over mountains and the rocky beds of dried-up rivers to win the votes of the Kalungas, subsistence farmers descended from fugitive slaves.

Ever since their forefathers fled from a gold mine and into the arid highlands of central Brazil 200 years ago, the Kalungas have come annually by donkey to a humble chapel where they baptise their childen and worship the Virgin Mary.

Many of the ancient traditions live on, including nighttime processions by a crowd singing softly and bearing slender branches tipped with burning beeswax. A local man, chosen to represent long-dead Portuguese emperors, is crowned.
But with the elections coming, folklore took second place to a week-long electoral binge.

Four rival candidates for mayor of the town of Cavalcante, a boneshaking five hours from the chapel by dirt track, descended on the festival armed with bottles of cachaca, a fiery sugar-cane spirit, and diesel generators to amplify the accordeon-and-drum bands brought in to sing their praises.

"People round here like public works, but what really counts is the personal touch. They're happier with a sack of rice," said Jorge Chein, a former mayor of Cavalcante whose wife, Celeste, is a front-runner this time around.
An estimated 100 million Brazilians go to the polls on Oct. 3 to choose between 100,000 would-be mayors and councilors standing in a first round of municipal elections.

Electioneering in cities like vast Sao Paulo may resemble that in U.S. or Europe. But in the backward interior, where many people cannot read or write, a sack of rice, bag of cement or box of medicine is the way to a voter's heart.

A priest making his annual visit to the Kalungas took a swipe at the electoral jollity during an evening Mass. "They say they've no money for schools and roads, but look how much they're spending on booze," he said.
The next day, in a fit of rage, he stormed out of a service and into a makeshift bar blaring music to harangue the tipsy revellers in a scene worthy of Brazilian soap opera.

"Pray, pray!" he yelled at two plump and perspiring woman dancers gyrating to a band. "This is a pilgrimage, and you're only here to drink cachaca and wiggle your behinds!" And he gave an energetic wiggle to his own, to the delight of some members of a campaign team.
Candidates' biggest challenge was making sure the mostly illiterate electorate knew how to vote.
"Don't forget, this is where you should put your cross, here, where my candidate's name is," one campaign worker repeated over and over as she handed out mock ballot slips.
Another distributed cards with his candidate's number cut out to be used as a stencil. "Now they can vote just as well as an intellectual," he joked.
Despite the campaigning, many of the Kalungas appeared to have decided already how to vote.

Maria Francisca dos Anjos waited for hours by the side of the dirt road before a candidate gave her and her six children a lift to the festival. "I'm voting for him," she said. "Who does me good gets my vote."
